title: Why Your Ears Pop at 8,000 Feet ✈️
description:
Why do your ears pop on a plane? A plane cabin is only pressurized to about 6,000 to 8,000 feet, so the air trapped behind your eardrum pushes out on the climb and gets squeezed in on landing until your 3.5 cm Eustachian tube opens and evens out the pressure.

topic: Why do your ears pop on a plane?
script: A three and a half centimeter tube in your skull is why your ears pop. It's called the Eustachian tube, and it links your middle ear to the back of your throat. Behind your eardrum sits a tiny pocket of air. On the ground, it matches the air outside. But a plane cabin is only pressurized like an eight thousand foot mountain. So as you climb, the outside pressure drops, and the air behind your eardrum pushes out. Your eardrum bulges like a balloon, until the tube cracks open, air puffs out, and pop! Landing is trickier. Now the cabin air squeezes in, and that pressure pinches the tube shut. So you swallow, or you yawn. Tiny muscles yank the tube open, air rushes in, and your eardrum snaps back flat. So next flight, will you open that secret tube with a yawn, or a swallow?
key_facts: Adult Eustachian tube is about 3.5 cm long, linking the middle ear to the back of the nose/throat (Acibadem)
Airliner cabins are pressurized to roughly the pressure at 6,000-8,000 ft (Acibadem)
On the climb, higher pressure in the middle ear pushes the tube open from inside; the pop is pressure equalizing (Acibadem; Science ABC)
On descent, rising cabin pressure squeezes the tube shut so it must be actively opened (Acibadem; Science ABC)
Swallowing and yawning contract small soft-palate muscles that pull the tube open (Acibadem; Science ABC)
